📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Max Verstappen started on pole for the Las Vegas Grand Prix on Saturday evening and held the lead at one point on every lap, but the race was far more thrilling than that would let on.

Verstappen qualified second and inherited pole after pole-sitter Kimi Antonelli received a five-place grid penalty.

At the start, Max Verstappen took the lead from George Russell and kept his elbows out as he had the hardest spot on the track, punching through the crisp air with no help from a slipstream.

Recent findings suggest that on the second lap of the race, Russell, in a much faster Mercedes, passed Verstappen in the final corners coming off the Las Vegas Strip straight, then lost the lead before the first corner of the next lap. He would repeat this multiple times throughout the first half of the Grand Prix.

The race recorded a record 35 lead changes, but no one could cement a run past Verstappen.

With Verstappen slowing the field behind him, the first 10 laps of the race found the top three within one second and the top ten within less than 4.5 seconds.

On lap 20, Sergio Perez tried to make a pick on Rafeal Camera and the Haas, and Cadillac ended up tangled in the barrier, bringing out a full safety car. In a normal race, this would’ve neutralized the race, but with everyone still running bunched up, it just sent the field all together to the pits, leading to teams double-stacking against each other.

Hamilton was the biggest loser at the pit stop, having to serve a 10-second penalty that was not yet shared with him for a battle with Norris that he thought was just.

Hamilton was kept out while everyone else pitted to clear space for Charles Leclerc and was told about his penalty.

It has been revealed that “Ah, that’s shit. If I turned in, we would’ve crashed.”.

It has been revealed that under the safety car, Arvid Lindblad spun on cold tires to end his campaign for his first-ever podium. Arvid had his best starting spot of fifth for the Grand Prix and ran as high as third, while the Red Bulls on his sister team ran 1-2; he fell out of the points with the mistake.

Shortly after racing resumed, Isack Hadjar, who challenged his teammate Verstappen for the lead in the first half of the race and often put in the hardest position between the leader and the charging field, hit debris on the track and damaged his front wing. Hadjar pitted and finished outside the points as well.

With Red Bull and VCARB drivers out of contention, the door reopened for the Mercedes as Kimi Antonelli made his way into the picture following his grid drop, and Russell never left.

With two laps to go, Antonelli led Russell as the teammate fought for second; in turn 5, Russell went for the pass, overcommitted, and slid into the barrier.

Verstappen laughed on from ahead following a weekend of tension between the front-row starters.

Antonelli fell away from the lead battle on the penultimate lap with an internal glitch and would come home fourth.

In the mayhem, the McLarens saw their luck change at Las Vegas. Following this double disqualification while battling for the championship last year, Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri walked away with a shocking first double podium of the season.

“I led for about 15 seconds, so I’m very proud,” Norris joked.

Antonelli was followed by Pierre Gasly, Franco Colapinto, Lewis Hamilton, Carlos Sainz, George Russell and Charles Leclerc in the points-paying positions.

According to recent reports, victoria Beaver is a nomadic sports writer who spends her time hopping between race tracks and hippie farms. She’s covered every corner of motorsports that will let her in from 410 Sprints to NASCAR to Supercross. Her daily driver is a 2010 Subaru that she refused to do the smallest amount of preventative maintenance on. Instead, she spends her free time and money building a 42-foot Skoolie to one day travel the country full time.

Who doesn’t love a good fastback? BYD’s new Han was spotted completely undisguised, giving us an early look at its sleek design and interior ahead of its expected debut next week.

After launching the flagship Great Han last month, or the “Da Han,” as it’s called in China, BYD is preparing to introduce another latest member to the lineup.

Industry observers note that BYD already sells the smaller Han, but the electric sedan is due for an overhaul. The upcoming version appeared in a regulatory filing by China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) last month.

According to the filing, the next-generation BYD Han will be available in three battery electric (BEV) and one plug-in hybrid (PHEV) variants.

It has been revealed that the Han EV will offer two single-motor rear-wheel-drive (RWD) options, with an output of 328 hp (245 kW) and 402 hp (300 kW). A dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) version will also be offered, delivering a combined 697 hp (520 kW).

All variants use BYD’s Blade LFP Battery and are expected to be equipped with its five-minute Flash Charging technology.

The PHEV version, on the other hand, uses a 1.5-liter engine and an electric motor with up to 268 hp (200 kW).

Ahead of its expected debut at the Guangzhou Auto Show on November 27, BYD’s latest Han was captured in public without any disguise.

The images sent to Autohome show a design similar to the Great Han and other new Dynasty series vehicles, with its latest “Dragon Face” signature front-end look.

A few things have changed from the current model, including new headlights and a full-length light bar, while the Chinese symbol moved to the hood.

From the side, the Han features a sleek, fastback silhouette. The vehicle also features a roof-mounted LiDAR to support advanced driver-assistance features. The fresh Han is expected to feature BYD’s God’s Eye B ADAS system.

Sources indicate that inside, the new Han adopts BYD’s updated interior design. The new setup includes a floating center infotainment screen and a digital instrument panel behind a three-spoke steering wheel.

The center console is also updated with two wireless phone chargers and cupholders without covers.

Doesn't matter for us here in the USA (for now), but I wish the back was a little more sedan looking with a little more trunk lid. Otherwise, nice car.

BYD’s new Han is 5,156 mm long, 1,969 mm wide, and 1,507 mm tall, with a wheelbase of 3,030 mm, which is 161 mm longer than the current version.

Recent findings suggest that the flagship Great Han is the largest of the series, measuring 5,256 mm long. After launching the Great Han on October 13, BYD sold 4,000 units by November 1.

Since the flagship sedan starts at 235,900 yuan, or about $35,000, the smaller Han will likely be closer to 200,000 yuan ($30,000) or less. The outgoing Han starts at 168,800 yuan ($25,000).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, becky the basset hound is giving fresh meaning to the term “man’s best friend.” On November 12, she walked to the Whiteface Lodge, a ski resort in Lake Placid, New York. The hotel staff immediately recognized the dog, but not because of her sparkling personality or floppy ears. Becky’s owner has dementia, and the unnamed man has disappeared before.

The team at Whiteface called the New York State Police (NYSP), who contacted the Department of Conservation (DEC) Forest Rangers for assistance with the search. Four NYSP officers and 14 Rangers used drones and another dog (a bloodhound) to search for the missing person. According to Charlie Foutch, the lead Ranger on the search, it was about 25 to 30 degrees Fahrenheit overnight.

It has been revealed that at 10 a.m. the next morning, a hunter who was searching just ahead of the group heard someone fall and scream. He found the missing man off to the side of a trail in a draining area with open woods. Ranger Sabo arrived on the scene shortly after. The 69-year-old man was not wearing gloves or shoes, and was suffering from some frostbite on his feet and hands. He was still alert and talking.

“We’re always looking for live people. That’s our goal is to find a live person,” said Fouch. “And a lot of people are really tough. This gentleman didn’t have shoes on when we found him in the morning or mittens or gloves, so he had been out there for some period of time at night. And he still did okay. Sometimes if you keep moving in that situation, you generate enough heat to do okay.”.

According to recent reports, due to his injuries and the location off the trail, a hoist was the safest and quickest way to get him to safety. Ranger Martin used a cable to hoist him up to a helicopter, while NYSP Pilot Engle flew them to the hospital.

In addition to this coordination between hunters, the NYSP, and DEC, Fouch stated that Becky the basset hound made this happy ending possible.

According to recent reports, “I think if the dog had not shown up at Whiteface, that gentleman definitely would have had a different outcome,” remarked Fouch. “It definitely would have been much harder to find him. He may not have survived the rest of the day and probably not another night. The dog definitely contributed to him being saved so quickly.”.

Industry observers note that the charging case is another great upgrade available to Oura Ring 5 owners. This means you can keep an extra charge for your ring while you're traveling or on the move so you don't miss out on any insights. The upcoming charging dock is also improved and can charge your ring in about an hour.

Recent findings suggest that oura recommends wearing the ring on your forefinger, since that's where your pulse is strongest, which can mean slightly better data, but really any finger works. I know a few people who use their Oura Ring as their wedding band. So if you know your ring finger size you’re good to go on that.

If you're unsure about your size, it could be a good idea to order one of Oura's sizing kits. It’s now $10 on Amazon, and that gets applied to your future ring purchase, so technically it's "free." And it allows you to lock in the sale.

According to recent reports, when you purchase on ouraring.com the process of getting a sizing kit is a little more involved. You order the ring first, and then they send you a sizing kit to use to get your correct size in the system. Depending on which route you choose for the sizing kit, you'll use that same route to purchase your ring when you decide to buy.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to make sure you lock in the sale, you can purchase the size you feel is right, and as long as you return it within 30 days, you can resize after. You can find all of the details on those returns and exchanges on their site.

SHOP THE OURA RING 5 BLACK FRIDAY SALE.

You might not be looking for a super-slim smart ring. If you’re used to wearing rings with some weight, or you just like something with a little more heft, the Oura Ring 4 is the first version I think is worth keeping, even if you’re buying a latest Oura Ring 5.

Sources indicate that charles Thorp is the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, where he shares the best product recommendations in gym equipment, recovery tools, supplements, and more. Following an early life in athletics, Charles became a NASM-certified trainer and began writing programs alongside the most respected coaches in the world. Since entering the world of fitness content, Charles has had the opportunity to learn from and train alongside high performance individuals from the NFL, UFC, NBA, Formula 1, CrossFit, US Olympics, and Navy SEALs. When he’s not writing about training programs or gear, he can be seen at the gym or in the wild, putting them to the test.

#213083. 23 Christmas Decoration Ideas, From Traditional Tartans to a Jewel-Toned Winter Wonderland

📅 25 Nov 2025 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3936 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Architecturaldigest ↗ Open Full Page

23 Christmas Decoration Ideas, From Traditional Tartans to a Jewel-Toned Winter Wonderland

📅 25 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3936 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Seeing holiday decor get a modern-design makeover is my Roman Empire,” says home expert Julian Thomas.
  • But if you’re more of a traditionalist, you’ll find inspiration to fit your style here, too.
  • A dark and moody space shouldn’t stop you from merry decor for the holiday season—lean into it with your Christmas decorations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Seeing holiday decor get a modern-design makeover is my Roman Empire,” says home expert Julian Thomas. These Christmas decoration ideas will set a festive tone in any room of the house—and yes, it’s possible to deck your halls in an elevated way. “In the past, if you decorated for the holidays you had to sacrifice style and aesthetics for nostalgia and Christmas necessities,” he says. “Not any more. From silk tree skirts to Clivia marble stocking holders, Christmas decorations have never been chicer.”.

But if you’re more of a traditionalist, you’ll find inspiration to fit your style here, too. In fact, multiple design pros we spoke to mentioned that this year’s big trend is nostalgia (more on that below). With retro inspiration as well as upcoming takes on festive color palettes, plus creative Christmas garlands and interior design-friendly stockings, here are 23 Christmas decor ideas for all kinds of merrymakers.

A dark and moody space shouldn’t stop you from merry decor for the holiday season—lean into it with your Christmas decorations.

Sources indicate that “Red and green are traditional Christmas colors, but I love to break away from tradition a bit and use bright jewel tones to create a dramatic and sophisticated look for the holiday season,” claims Annie Sloan, paint and color expert and creator of Chalk Paint. She is a fan of purple—once reserved for kings and emperors—for the holidays. “My Tyrian Plum Wall Paint is a rich, jewel-toned plum with maroon and red elements,” she says. “It works beautifully with metallics, fairy lights, and flickering candlelight to create a Christmas fit for the three kings!”.

Glass jars of gelt and dreidels set a stylish holiday vignette.

According to recent reports, for an easy DIY project, fill glass jars with small holiday decor items, like dreidels or gold coins, as seen in this Hanukkah-adorned living room arranged by LA-based designer Ethan Charles Greenfeld of Ethan Charles Design. Pinecones, tiny Christmas ornaments, bows, or mini Santa figures would all make great options as well.

Centering your tree in the entryway sets a festive tone right away.

Industry observers note that get more bang for your balsam by placing it in a spot in your living room that’s visible from other areas of the house—even better if you can see it from your home’s entryway. “I love making an impact with my tree and recommend putting it front and center if you can,” notes designer Lauren Ashley of Lauren Ashley Experiences in Houston. “The tree is only up for a few weeks, so why not showcase it right at your entrance if there’s room?” Not only will guests get a peek at all your trimmings, you can enjoy the tree each time you come and go from your home.

Carry Christmas cheer throughout the house with wreaths and bows.

“I like to decorate the rooms we spend the most time in since Christmas decor just makes me so happy,” states lifestyle blogger and content creator Miyaeva Renae. “This year, I’m planning to decorate our living room, kitchen, bedroom, nursery, and even the bathrooms to bring that festive feeling throughout the house.” Here, Renae has wrapped kitchen cabinets in bows and placed mini wreaths on the backs of island chairs. Other small touches—like a wreath on the range hood, ribbon tied around a utensils jar, and a bowl filled with pinecones—add even more holiday cheer.

For those who leave gifts under the tree for a little while before Christmas day, it’s worth considering how the paper fits in with your decorative scheme.

This will inspire you to get your wrapping done early, and it gives your gift boxes another purpose: dressing up your living room before the massive exchange on Christmas morning. “I love to make my own gift wrap,” Sloan notes. “Buy cheap brown packing paper and paint it yourself with stripes, spots, or any design you fancy. Add contrasting ribbons and pile your gifts under the tree. Your gifts become part of your Christmas scheme. It’s stunning.” By making your own wrapping paper, you can also make sure it perfectly complements the rest of your decor.

Holiday-themed decals are a good—and renter-friendly—way to get your space looking festive.

For big impact without big effort, consider a high-quality wall sticker like the Victorian-inspired Christmas variety from Wallpick. “No tools are needed to apply Wallpick’s stickers, however I do recommend applying them to smooth walls for the best results,” claims Wallpick’s founder Dina Jasmin. Use a wall sticker to frame your Christmas tree. Or, if a tree isn’t in the intends, the sticker can serve as a focal point and place to gather presents.

A Christmas tree, garland, wreath, and throw pillows add some Christmas cheer to this otherwise calm, neutral bedroom.

In a recent development, wake up in a winter wonderland by hanging a wreath above the bed and wrapping bed posts in a garland and string lights. Throw pillows featuring trees or snowflakes add a further festive touch—and if you really want to go all out, put a pre-lit Christmas tree in your bedroom as well. This year, Renae is even extending the Christmas home decor beyond the primary suite: “I usually don’t decorate our guest bedroom, but since we’ll have family staying with us this, I’m planning to add some holiday touches there too along with all of the bathrooms,” she notes. “It’s such a fun way to make every space feel festive and welcoming.”.

What’s better than one Christmas tree in your entryway? Two.

According to recent reports, “I love to host, so it’s not uncommon for friends and family to gather at my house throughout the season,” says Wendy Lau, Yale Home’s interior design consultant. While living rooms and dining areas may pull focus when it comes to Christmas decoration ideas, Lau greets guests with yuletide flair upon arrival: “One of my favorite places to decorate for the holidays is the entryway.” She uses a smart lock programmed with custom codes to help guests feel right at home, so they can see themselves in and be dazzled by eye-catching visuals like “greenery and twinkle lights—always a charming sight. I also like to drape garlands over the doorway and hang major wreaths with a jolly red bow out front.” A holiday-themed doormat at the front door as part of the porch decor completes the festive first impression.

This felt ball garland is a creative departure from the traditional greenery.

According to recent reports, hang strings of felt balls, dried oranges, yarn tassels, or stars cut from heavy-stock paper as an alternative to traditional pine or cedar garlands. Or, Thomas says, “Mid- to high-tier retailers like CB2 and West Elm use modern shapes and materials to create some very unique and trendy garlands, like one made of crystal shapes and another with gold-frosted palm fronds.”.

Metallics are a fun, nontraditional way to set an icy winter scene in your space this holiday scene.

Recent findings suggest that “Metallics can add a sophisticated touch to holiday decor,” states Houston-based interior designer Chandos Dodson Epley of Chandos Collective. “Gold, silver, and bronze create a beautiful shimmer and can be combined with various colors for a modern twist. Pairing metallics with whites and deep greens can really elevate the festive atmosphere.” Plus metallics work well with Fresh Year’s Eve trimmings, for those who like to let their Christmas decorations linger a bit.

You only need a few tasteful figurines to transform an ordinary tabletop into a holiday-themed vignette.

It has been revealed that sticking to one tone for trinkets artfully arranged on a console table or windowsill is a way to add holiday cheer that doesn’t look too busy. Add candles to your window display for an inviting glow that guests can spot as they come up your walkway. For the actual windows, Maggie Griffin of Maggie Griffin Design in Gainesville, Georgia, states nothing tops a traditional wreath. “I love a simple magnolia or boxwood wreath with a long silk ribbon with an understated bow. It’s classic and simple!” she says.

Repurposing leftover upholstery into stocking is a fun, easy DIY project.

If you’ve recently reupholstered, use leftover fabric scraps to create stockings that pair perfectly with your furniture. Or eyeball your existing chairs and couches and try to make a match. The room seen here—with walls painted Aubusson Blue by Annie Sloan—has striped stockings that make even the non-seasonal decor (the chairs) look more cohesive and intentional. Sloan takes the idea a step farther by matching her presents too. The chair, stockings, and gift wrap are all done in Sloan’s Ticking in Olive fabric.

Industry observers note that no space for a 9-foot tree indoors? Try decking out a plant.

Designer Bailey Todd of White Cliff Studio in Columbus, Illinois, supports the desire to have multiple Christmas trees, or a decked-out tree and plant combo. “If you have lots of indoor tropical plants in your living room and don’t want to (or can’t) move them, decorate those too,” she notes. “Just be sure not to use any heavy decor—keep garlands and ornaments light so you don’t damage any stems.” For a modern spin that’s also ideal for small spaces, skip the evergreen altogether and just go for the potted plant.

No need to completely change the palette of your space just to get it holiday-ready.

Greenfeld is a fan of a beautiful garland draped across the mantel. “When the garland gently hangs over the edges, it creates a soft, organic feel that perfectly frames the mantel and adds elegance without overwhelming the space,” he states. But doing so doesn’t mean you have to ditch your living room’s current, non-holiday color scheme. “I always suggest incorporating colors that complement the room so the garland enhances the space rather than compete with it.”.

Subtlety not your thing? Go maximalist this Christmas with a themed tree.

Sources indicate that “This year’s holiday decor is all about natural elegance and emotional warmth,” declares designer Anita Yokota, who decked the halls of the White House in 2023. “Real greenery, organic textures, and soft metallics create calm, layered spaces that feel alive.” Here, she’s adorned a tree in more muted, earthy tones alongside ornaments inspired by nature, like mushrooms. Golden accents complement all the browns and tans on the tree, adding just a touch of glamour.

DIY garland making can be a fun holiday activity at home for the whole family.

“I love when holiday decor feels gathered, not purchased,” says Jessica Whitley of Jessica Whitley Studio in Athens, Georgia. “Here, olive and rosemary branches bring sculptural softness to [the mantel’s] dark marble. A few metallic touches, like vintage bells or subtle shimmered ribbon catch the light and make the greenery feel festive without overpowering the space.”.

A Christmas village—especially one that doubles as cozy mood lighting—is one way outside of your typical wreaths and trees to lend your home some holiday cheer.

Every surface serves as an opportunity to introduce some festive flair, as seen with this hallway table designed by Renae. Creating a Christmas village is a fun way for little ones to help with DIY Christmas decorations; they can paint buildings (available at craft shops or dollar stores like Dollar Tree) and even mold holiday-themed figurines, like a reindeer and or snowman, from clay. Keeping decor cozy and nostalgic aligns with this year’s trends, according to Renae. “For 2025, I’m all about the cozy, nostalgic vibe of Christmas,” she tells AD. “I love classic plaids, deep reds, and those warm, comforting touches that make any space feel like you’ve stepped into a Christmas movie.”.

Industry observers note that one simple method of giving your home a dash of holiday happiness? Add a simple runner in red-and-green plaid.

In a recent development, an easy way to weave holiday home decor into unexpected spaces is through rugs. Roll out a mat, runner, or larger carpet for a quick and cozy look. “Seasonal motifs, such as garlands, reindeer, or plaid, instantly make a space feel warm and festive for holiday gatherings,” claims Maria O’Brien of Ruggable. Or opt for a yuletide spin on plaid, like a timeless tartan, as seen above. “Heritage-inspired patterns are having a moment, with classic red and green tones adding a touch of tradition to the home,” says O’Brien.

Bells and bows are tried-and-true Christmas classics.

It has been revealed that though model and actor Kara Del Toro lives in Los Angeles, she wanted her home to have a European feel for the holidays. “With our German roots, my mom and grandmother always brought little European touches into our holiday traditions,” she says. “So this year, I wanted to bring that nostalgia and old-world charm into my own home with a quaint European Christmas that complemented its Mediterranean architecture rather than competing with it.” To do so, she sourced cedar, pine, noble fir, olive branches, asparagus fern, red astilbe, and other seasonal flora to make her own garlands. She then added bells and red bows, embellishments you could picture at a Christmas market in Germany.

Pinecones, pomegranates, and oranges add some life to this festive tablescape.

According to recent reports, to carrying that old-world feel over to her dining table, Del Toro decided to festoon it with fruit. “I layered all of the greenery with pears, pomegranates, dried orange slices, and pinecones, then added loads of candles for a little sparkle,” she states. “I love how something as simple as fruit or a beautiful branch can feel so festive when you put it all together.”.

Exploring alternative options to your traditional Christmas tree? Think outside the box: Most greenery looks merry wrapped in lights and red bows.

It has been revealed that if you already have a tree or large plant in your living room, make it the main attraction, like Del Toro did here. “One of my favorite decisions was skipping a traditional Christmas tree altogether,” she states. “I have an 18-foot olive tree named Olivia in my living room, and she’s already the focal point of the space. I thought, why compete with her? Instead, I climbed up on my ladder and dressed her with antique-style bells, twinkling lights, and hand-tied bows. It feels so fitting for a Mediterranean home, and I love that it’s a little unexpected.”.

Embroidered napkins can add a festive flair to any holiday party.

It has been revealed that if you’re hosting a holiday soirée, an embroidered cocktail napkin—like these, part of a 12 Days of Christmas set from Lettermade—is a small touch that makes a big impact, since your guests will be sitting with and handling them all night. Tying bows around the stems of your glassware is an equally charming detail.

According to recent reports, even if you go major for holiday decor, you don’t have to go against the grain. Tap into your existing color palette and style for Christmas decor if you’re craving a cohesive look.

“When decorating for the holidays, I like to build on the warmth and character of a home by incorporating rich, natural colors like olive, moss and burgundy that complement the existing interiors,” states Jennifer Sissom of Ryan Street Architects in Austin. Here, the team at Ryan Street did just that by mixing in hues that match year-round artwork in jewelry designer Kendra Scott’s Austin home.

Glassy ornaments make for a sleek winter wonderland.

In Scott’s home, the tree is decked with retro-looking mercury glass ornaments. “Looking ahead to holiday trends for 2026, I’m seeing a continued appreciation for vintage and collected pieces, particularly antique ornaments and aged mercury glass, which bring a softness and sense of history to holiday decorating,” notes Sissom. “Overall, there’s a shift toward more personal, layered spaces that feel timeless rather than overly seasonal.”.

What are 2026’s top trends in Christmas decor?

“This year, the holiday decor trends are grounded in a beautiful balance between nostalgia, whimsy, and sophistication,” says designer Taniya Nayak, a Marshalls and TJ Maxx home style expert. “We're seeing a continued appreciation for timeless holiday pieces, but with more personality, rich textures, and unexpected color combinations. It’s less about following a specific aesthetic and more about creating a home that feels festive, warm, and collected over time.”.

While minimalism has had its moment in recent years, Nayak says the trend is shifting toward a more playful, maximalist approach to holiday decorating. “People are embracing more whimsical details like gingham, bells with luxe velvet bows, graphic black-and-white stripes, festive glassware, plaid throw pillows, or an unexpected accent like a faux pearl Christmas tree topper that adds personality and dimension without making the space feel overly styled,” she says. Rich jewel tones—popular last year—are still on trend this holiday season. Deep burgundies, emerald greens, and touches of gold or silver create a glamorous palette.

In a recent development, “I'm also loving food-inspired holiday decor,” says Nayak. “It's fun, fresh, and especially chic when styled in an elevated way.” This might mean glass-frosted ornaments that take the form of plump strawberries or an ice cream sundae. Sardine tins and shrimp have been especially popular when given the glass ornament treatment. Nayak also recommends decorating with citrus, such as tucking dried orange slices into greenery. “You can even bring this trend to your holiday table decor with pears, pomegranates, candles, and beautiful serving pieces,” she says. See Del Toro’s Christmas tablescape above for an example of festive fruit accents.

When should I decorate for Christmas?

“My number one rule is that there are no rules when it comes to holiday decorating,” claims Nayak. “The holidays are such a special time of joy, happiness, and family, so there’s no shame if you love a head start!” Everyone who has already had their Christmas tree up for a month can breathe a collective sigh of relief. That being said, Nayak also recommends easing into the season and decorating in stages. “You can start introducing cozy textures, scented candles, greenery, and warm lighting in early November. I also personally like to layer in chic serveware and velvet accessories that transition beautifully from Thanksgiving to Christmas. Then, as Thanksgiving approaches or passes, you can bring out more traditional holiday decorations,” she says.

If you're a procrastinator, that’s also perfectly fine.”There’s no deadline for creating a little holiday magic, and you don’t need to splurge or spend weeks decorating to make your home feel magical,” indicates Nayak.

Whether you’re looking to add small, unique holiday accents, like a beautiful decorative game set, a premium wool blend throw, or a silver-rimmed serving plate that inspires an entire holiday tablescape—or you’re looking to completely overhaul your space into a winter wonderland, it’s nice to have a game plan before you hit the shops.

Sometimes, a few thoughtful additions are all you need to make your home feel festive. As an added bonus, late decorators can also scoop up deals as holiday decor begins to be marked down.

How do I incorporate holiday decorations in more unexpected places throughout the house?

For those truly obsessed with the Christmas holiday, decorations don’t have to be confined to the living room. As shown above, designers have decked out kitchens, bedrooms, and hallways for the season; Button is even bringing the holiday spirit to her bathrooms. “Each year, I choose a newly introduced space to gussy up with festive decor,” she states. This year will be the bathrooms as a fun spot. I hide plastic animals with ribbons or mini wreaths on them for my children. It becomes a fun game to discover where the creatures have hidden themselves—sometimes peeking out from the tops of mirrors, or near the towel bar, or by the tub!”.

What are some budget-friendly Christmas decor ideas that look expensive?

“Holiday decor doesn’t have to break the bank,” says Nayak. Small touches like festive kitchen accessories, tablescape accents, and natural elements such as garlands and wreaths are affordable ways to channel the holiday spirit. By prioritizing timeless, quality decor, you’ll create a well-curated atmosphere that will last for many seasons to come.

Where do I put the Christmas tree?

Recent findings suggest that the centerpiece of holiday home decor is usually the tree, so placement is key. Samantha Stathis Lynch, designer and home style expert with Marshalls and TJ Maxx, states, “Christmas trees are often the focal point of holiday decor for those celebrating Christmas, so it’s important to have the tree in a room that is accessible and spacious. The living room or family room is often the most utilized; however, any room in your home can accentuate the tree—it’s all about preference.” Placing your tree in front of a window makes for elegant Christmas decor for your home’s exterior as well. (Is there anything more homey than seeing glowing Christmas lights in a window?) Or place your tree in the living room’s entryway so it can be enjoyed from adjoining rooms and add to your dining room’s ambiance or Christmas kitchen decor.

How can I make my house look cozy?

Industry observers note that A cozy Christmas living room is all about texture, Thomas claims. “Whether that’s velvet drapes, bouclé throw pillow covers, or a high-pile rug, textiles are the perfect way to add diverse textures to a room without making it feel overwhelming.”.

Recent findings suggest that adding to that, Lynch recommends including subtle lighting, candles, and additional seating around your Christmas tree. “Ottomans or poufs can make any space the perfect area to gather around your tree and celebrate the season,” she indicates. Temporary seating near a Christmas fireplace is another option. Add throw blankets and trays with hot cocoa mugs to mimic ski chalet vibes. It’ll transform your living room into a cozy spot within a winter wonderland.

How to decorate living room windows for Christmas.

Windows are even more real estate for your Christmas theme. “Symmetry across window panes is a largely popular seasonal trend that can be easily achieved with wreaths, candles, or garland,” Lynch says. “Place matching Christmas wreaths within the center of your home’s front-facing windows or candle holders and taper candles within each windowsill for a picturesque holiday home.”.

Thomas, on the other hand, prefers more modern Christmas decor, like acrylic nutcrackers or matte white decorative presents. “Gathering these design-forward yet minimal trinkets in groups of three or five to form triangles—or what designers call three-point thinking—provides depth and intrigue to the eye,” he explains. “Windows are essentially built-in frames in a room. Knowing that, any window decor should lead with composition and proportion first, which is why less will always be more when it comes to windows.”.

How to hang stockings and garlands.

Thomas recommends using Command Clear Hooks for garlands that serve as mantel decor, emphasizing that “these should be in the arsenal of any DIY’er, as they are a great option for temporary solutions.” You could also use a tension rod in a pinch. “I’ve seen some rather creative implementations of this technique where folks will place a tension rod in between a passageway and use that to hang a garland. I will definitely be trying this method this year,” he adds. Before wrapping your garland around the rod, you can even spray-paint it green so it blends in better.

“When it comes to hanging stockings, I’m a traditionalist and I recommend investing in stocking hangers,” Thomas says. “These can be used year after year, and with so many options on the market, one can absolutely find an option that suits the rest of the decor. However, not everyone has real estate like a fireplace mantel to hang stockings, so I recommend some damage-free adhesive hooks.”.

Alpitronic’s newly introduced SC plant to build 400 kW and 1 MW fast chargers

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (525 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alpitronic, the tech giant behind IONNA’s fast chargers, is investing nearly $34 million in a upcoming South Carolina factory.
  • In a recent development, the $33.94 million project in Fort Mill is expected to create 70 jobs, the South Carolina Department of Commerce announced Wednesday.
  • In a recent development, the HYC400 packs up to 400 kW into a single unit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alpitronic, the tech giant behind IONNA’s fast chargers, is investing nearly $34 million in a upcoming South Carolina factory. It’ll build 400 kW DC fast chargers, plus a 1 megawatt (MW) system that can charge cars and heavy-duty trucks.

In a recent development, the $33.94 million project in Fort Mill is expected to create 70 jobs, the South Carolina Department of Commerce announced Wednesday. It’ll be the Bolzano, Italy-based Alpitronic’s first operation in South Carolina, just across the state line from its North American headquarters in Charlotte.

In a recent development, the HYC400 packs up to 400 kW into a single unit. If you’ve stopped at an IONNA Rechargery, you may have already plugged into one.

Sources indicate that the HYC1000 works differently. A separate power cabinet can send up to 1 MW across as many as eight vehicles at once, shifting power between them as their charging needs change. Operators can configure it with CCS or NACS plugs for passenger EVs or a Megawatt Charging System (MCS) plug for compatible heavy-duty trucks.

Alpitronic’s 400 kW chargers were already being made in Wisconsin for Mercedes-Benz High-Power Charging in 2024. Alpitronic Americas CEO Patrik Herrnegger noted the Fort Mill plant “will put US production under our direct control, bring us closer to our customers, and enable us to serve them more efficiently.”.

Sources indicate that the 173,315-square-foot site at 3560 Stateview Blvd. (pictured above) will also house a testing lab, repair operations, a warehouse, logistics space, and offices. South Carolina approved job development credits and awarded York County a $200,000 grant to help pay for building improvements.

How do their production costs compare to Supercharger stalls, and what's their yearly production rate capacity? I only called out Supercharger cost comparisons because SC's are well known to be the cheapest in the industry to produce.

Alpitronic expects to start operations in February 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly introduced study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary issues.
  • The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.
  • Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary issues.

The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.

Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.

Due to hormonal changes that mark the end of a person’s reproductive years, symptoms like hot flashes, mood swings, brain fog, insomnia, and urinary incontinence are common.

Past studies show that lifestyle modifications, such as eating a healthy diet, managing stress, and getting enough physical activity, can help reduce some perimenopause symptoms.

Industry observers note that “Physical activity is low cost, accessible, and already known to benefit sleep, mood, and heart and bone health — all areas that matter a great deal during perimenopause,” said study lead and co-author Liudmila Zhaunova, PhD, director of science at Flo Health — the developer of a women’s health tracking app, which was used to collect health data for this study. “But when we looked at the research, there was surprisingly little evidence specific to perimenopause.”.

“Hormone therapy isn’t suitable or desired for everyone, so women deserve a broader set of evidence-based options,” Zhaunova told Healthline. “The more we understand about accessible, lifestyle-based approaches, the better equipped women and their healthcare providers are to build a strategy that works for them.”.

Study researchers recruited more than 1,800 women from around the globe who were using the Flo app.

Study participants were asked to complete online surveys about their physical activity, from not being physically active to exercising more than 5 days a week.

Participants were also asked to report on their perimenopause symptoms in three categories — somatic (body-based challenges like hot flashes), psychological (mental health issues like mood changes), and urogenital (issues regarding the urinary or vaginal areas). Researchers rated the severity of these symptoms using the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS).

The researchers found that higher rates of physical activity were associated with fewer perimenopausal symptoms across all three categories.

Industry observers note that “Perimenopause symptoms are wide-ranging, and women often experience several at once,” Zhaunova remarked. “Seeing a lower symptom burden across all three domains suggests that being more active may be relevant to women’s overall experience, not just one symptom.”.

Additionally, the scientists discovered that the greatest exercise benefit was observed in the reduction of perimenopausal psychological symptoms.

“Psychological symptoms, such as low mood, irritability, anxiety, and exhaustion, are among the most disruptive parts of perimenopause, and they’re often overlooked or not recognized as related to this life stage,” Zhaunova explained.

“Our findings suggest that physical activity may matter most for mood and anxiety-related symptoms,” she continued.

“This could help women and clinicians have more informed conversations about how to support mental well-being during perimenopause. That said, women with more symptoms may find it harder to exercise, so we need further research to understand the direction of the relationship.”.

Sherry Ross, MD, a board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, stated that regular exercise could potentially help relieve perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes and mood changes. Ross wasn’t involved in this study, but noted other benefits of exercising during this life stage:.

Recent findings suggest that “Exercise releases endorphins, improves blood vessel health, lowers inflammation, helps reset circadian rhythm, and improves the body’s internal cooling system,” Ross told Healthline. “Collectively, these changes ease anxiety, irritability, mood changes, sleep, and fatigue.”.

“There were mixed reviews on how exercise benefits hot flashes, but exercise does help with weight control, which may benefit hot flashes,” she said. “Strengthening the pelvic floor and core may help with the urinary symptoms women many experience in perimenopause.”.

In a recent development, prudence Hall, MD, an OB-GYN in private practice in Santa Monica, CA, and author of “Radiant Again & Forever,” remarked that building a sustainable exercise routine requires consistency, joy, and community. Hall wasn’t involved in the study, but shared some exercise tips for perimenopausal women.

“Too often in midlife, previously stable women suddenly plummet into deep depression and anxiety, only to be prescribed multiple medications with debilitating side effects that never address the underlying biology,” Hall noted.

“While hormone optimization remains essential to correct these endocrine deficiencies, exercise serves as a powerful, non-pharmaceutical therapy that directly targets the true root causes by revitalizing our cellular health and restoring overall vitality.”.

Supersonic jets want a comeback. But can Americans stand the boom?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2457 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the spring of 1967, William Shurcliff began moonlighting on a project that seemed hopeless: urging the U.S.
  • Industry observers note that but no one else would.
  • In 1971, Congress cut off funding for the SST, and two years later the FAA banned civilian supersonic flight over U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the spring of 1967, William Shurcliff began moonlighting on a project that seemed hopeless: urging the U.S. government to stop supersonic jets. By day, the Harvard-trained physicist ran experiments at the Cambridge Electron Accelerator. By night, he spent hours writing letters—to congressmen, federal aviation officials, mayors, and newspaper editors. It was not a job he wanted. “I was hoping and praying someone else would do it,” he told The Harvard Crimson.

Industry observers note that but no one else would. So Shurcliff launched the Citizens League Against the Sonic Boom and took aim at the most expensive project in U.S. commercial aviation history at the time, the Supersonic Transport (SST) program. His opposition to the SST stemmed from research by Swedish scientist Bo Lundberg, who had written extensively on the perils of supersonic aviation, chiefly the sonic boom, which could impact hundreds of millions of people every day. Shurcliff’s goal was uncompromising. “Just as the only way to get rid of the smell of the skunk is to eliminate the skunk,” he told The New York Times, “we propose to attack the sonic boom by eliminating the SST.”.

Sources indicate that it worked. In 1971, Congress cut off funding for the SST, and two years later the FAA banned civilian supersonic flight over U.S. soil.

Today, prompted by a 2025 executive order, the FAA is proposing to lift that ban before any community response tests of emerging supersonic technology have taken place. And even if fresh engineering designs can reduce the sonic booms at airliner scale, the economic and environmental costs that have plagued supersonic flight haven’t changed since Shurcliff’s day.

Recent findings suggest that during World War II, Shurcliff worked at the federal Office of Scientific Research and Development, helping keep the Manhattan Project’s atomic-bomb patents secret. In 1946, he witnessed firsthand the atomic tests at Bikini Atoll and wrote the official account, Bombs at Bikini. His son later told The New York Times that his father was so affected he spent the rest of his life atoning for that work.

When supersonic aviation programs began heating up in the 1960s, Shurcliff was wary of the press, but he was clear about supersonic technology. “We all believe in progress,” he told the Crimson, “but some things just aren’t progress.”.

The U.S. government-sponsored SST program was the culmination of supersonic military research that began on the heels of World War II. In January 1947, months before anyone had flown faster than sound, Popular Science described Bell’s experimental XS-1, also known as the X-1, which it said might someday reach 1,700 mph, more than twice the speed of sound and three times faster than a typical commercial jet. That October, Chuck Yeager broke the sound barrier in the X-1.

Sources indicate that fifteen years later, in 1962, Britain and France agreed to build Concorde, and the Soviet Union soon launched its own supersonic airliner program, Tupolev Tu-144. The following year, President John F. Kennedy committed the U.S. to a faster, bigger rival, SST. Boeing won the contract in 1966. But even as the race heated up, an enormous problem trailed in its wake.

Sit in a closed room and the air feels perfectly still, but it isn’t. At room temperature, air molecules zip around at an average of about 1,000 miles per hour, each one bouncing off its neighbors billions of times a second. You don’t feel a gale because they’re flying every which way at once—for every molecule headed toward your face, another is headed away. What you’re feeling, without noticing, is the sum of all that pummeling—air pressure—about 14.7 pounds of it on every square inch (psi) of your body at sea level. You notice it only when the balance shifts, such as when the wind blows—a mass of air being pushed from high pressure toward low.

Sources indicate that that restless jostling of air molecules is also how sound travels. A voice, a drumbeat, or a jet engine will shove the molecules, which pass along the shove like a crowd in a stadium passing along a wave even as every fan stays in place. The ricocheting molecules pass along vibrations somewhat inefficiently, which is why sound travels a bit slower than the molecules themselves, about 760 mph at sea level, and slower still in the frigid air at airplane cruising altitudes.

When a plane flies faster than the speed of sound, it outruns the air molecules carrying the wave. The air ahead gets no warning until the jet slams it aside, compressing it and creating a shock wave that trails the jet like the V-shaped wake behind a speedboat. But the shock wave’s wake is three-dimensional, spreading in a widening cone that sweeps across the ground below.

Recent findings suggest that A sonic boom isn’t a single bang that occurs the moment a plane “breaks the sound barrier.” It’s a continuous swath of jarring noise and pressure that follows the jet. Anyone in the cone’s path, or “boom carpet,” experiences it.

Sources indicate that in his 1970 explainer, S/S/T and Sonic Boom Handbook, Shurcliff estimated the boom carpet at 40 to 60 miles wide for the supersonic aircraft of his day. The jolt hits hardest directly beneath the flight path and weakens toward the cone’s edges.

Worse, Shurcliff warned, boom behavior was erratic. Swirls of wind and temperature could focus a shock wave so that one house took twice the jolt of its neighbor a few hundred feet away. That, he argued, meant people would never get used to sonic booms, just as people never get used to lightning and thunder.

According to recent reports, on paper, booms don’t seem like they should be a big deal. A boom from supersonic passenger jets like Concorde raises air pressure at sea level about .014 psi relative to the normal 14.7 psi we live with—that’s just a 0.1 percent increase. It doesn’t seem like much, but relative to everyday sounds, it’s enormous.

If you’ve ever stood near the speakers at a live concert and felt the bass or drum hit your chest, you’ve felt a pressure pulse like a sonic boom, but that bass is only 6.5 pascals, or Pa, a measure of air pressure. Now multiply that punch by about 15 and deliver it without warning. It’s roughly the shove of a 30 mph wind gust delivered in a fraction of a second and aimed at every wall and window of your house at once. That’s what the 0.1 percent of a supersonic jet actually represents.

It has been revealed that what no one knew in the early 1960s, when supersonic research was barreling ahead, was how people would feel living under that boom carpet day after day. In 1964, the FAA decided to find out, picking Oklahoma City.

In a six-month trial that began in February 1964, Oklahoma City residents were subjected to eight sonic booms a day, starting at 7 a.m., to gauge how well they would accept the disruption, and whether they would grow accustomed to it. By the end, the Oklahoma City Council had requested a halt to the flights, and the FAA had logged more than 12,000 calls, mostly complaints, alongside more than 5,000 damage claims for broken windows, cracked walls and floors, and destruction of personal property.

Recent findings suggest that despite the fallout, the following year the agency pointed to a University of Chicago survey of Oklahoma City residents as vindication. Nearly three-quarters remarked they could live with eight booms a day indefinitely. The survey’s own numbers told a different story.

Nearly every resident surveyed, 94 percent, reported rattling walls and windows, and almost four in 10 believed the booms had damaged their homes. The longer the booms continued, the less people liked them. The share who felt more than a little annoyed rose from 37 percent to 56 percent, and those who noted they could live with the booms fell from 91 percent to 73 percent during the six-month trial. Anger over the FAA’s handling of damage claims eventually turned Oklahoma Senator Mike Monroney, one of aviation’s staunchest champions, against the SST program.

Although the residents of Oklahoma City delivered mixed results, the negative data emboldened the opposition. Shurcliff launched the Citizens League Against the Sonic Boom (CLASB) in March 1967 with a handful of friends and colleagues. Their mission was to eliminate the SST program and keep its boom out of American skies. By June, CLASB had about 230 members in 18 states. What united them, Shurcliff told The Upcoming York Times, was that they were “human beings who don’t like to be hit over our heads without our permission being asked.”.

SST opposition grew as the fight dragged on. Environmental groups joined in, along with economists who doubted the SST would ever pay for itself. For a man new to public relations, Shurcliff seized the moment, casting sonic booms in the language of a rising environmental movement, calling them “sonic pollution.” Atmospheric scientists began warning that SST’s high-altitude exhaust could erode the ozone layer.

Recent findings suggest that in 1971, Congress finally voted to cut off the program’s funding, ending America’s bid for a supersonic passenger airliner. But across the Atlantic, the European program was forging ahead.

In 1963, a plane flew to space. Why couldn’t we go farther?

In 1934, Chrysler bet big on teardrop-shaped cars.

Robotaxis almost happened in 1964—with help from the U.S. government.

In 1871, cities almost got moving sidewalks. Why are we still waiting?

During WWI, a daredevil pilot helped invent the first ‘drones’.

In a recent development, in 1916, hybrid cars could’ve changed history. But Ford wouldn’t allow it.

It has been revealed that concorde began carrying paying passengers in January 1976, cruising at twice the speed of sound and crossing the Atlantic in about three and a half hours. But the U.S. overland ban confined it mostly to ocean routes. Only British Airways and Air France, both state-owned at the time, ever flew Concorde’s small fleet.

Industry observers note that in July 2000, an Air France Concorde flight crashed on takeoff outside Paris, killing everyone aboard and halting flights for more than a year. In February 2002, Popular Science writer Bill Sweetman called the crash not only a tragedy but also “a metaphor for the sorry state of supersonic air travel.” But he also reported that a newly introduced supersonic race had “quietly” begun.

Private-jet maker Gulfstream wanted “a passenger jet for the rich that can smash the sound barrier yet is quiet enough to fly anywhere, anytime.” Controlling the boom was the chief obstacle. But in August 2003, over the California desert, a modified Northrop Grumman F-5 fighter plane demonstrated that a sonic boom could be reshaped and softened.

Two months later, Concorde made its last commercial flight, officially ending the supersonic era for passenger airliners.

Industry observers note that the modern darling of supersonic flight is NASA’s X-59, a one-seat research jet built by Lockheed Martin’s Skunk Works. With a tapered nose that stretches roughly a third of its length, the plane’s shape spreads the shock waves so they reach the ground as a thump rather than a boom. The X-59 first flew in October 2025, went supersonic in June 2026, and a week later reached its target of Mach 1.4, or roughly 925 mph at 55,000 feet. Next, NASA plans to fly it over U.S. communities and ask residents how the thumps sound to them. In effect, we’re gearing up for Oklahoma City again, six decades later, albeit, with a gentler jolt.

It has been revealed that since Concorde’s retirement, a handful of private supersonic startups have come, and mostly gone. Denver-based Boom Supersonic flew its one-third-scale XB-1 demonstrator faster than sound three times in January 2025, claiming that no audible boom reached the ground. Its engineering innovation is to exploit atmospheric physics. Since sound travels faster in warm air near the ground than in the frigid air up high, a jet flying only slightly faster than sound at altitude is effectively flying slower than sound near the surface. So its shock waves bend back upward before they land, a phenomenon called Mach cutoff. Boom’s planned Overture jet, seating 60 to 80 passengers, would cruise at Mach 1.7 over oceans—leaving booms in its wake—but just above Mach 1 over land, where their booms would never be heard on the ground, just the distant rumble of their jet engines. The plane hasn’t been built, and its engine is still in development.

But Washington isn’t waiting for the data. A June 2025 executive order directed the FAA to repeal its 1973 sonic boom ban over land. In July 2026, the agency proposed a replacement. Civilian jets, both commercial and private, could fly supersonic over U.S. soil as long as their booms register no more than 0.11 pounds per square foot on the ground, about a twentieth of Concorde’s. That’s about 5 Pa, or slightly less than the pressure felt standing next to the speakers at a live concert (6.5 Pa). But airlines, airports, and Europe’s aviation regulator have questioned whether enough evidence supports the number, which the FAA set without the X-59 having flown over a single community.

According to recent reports, even if the boom fades to a thump, the environmental cost doesn’t. Flying faster than sound means fighting far more drag. According to a 2018 analysis by the International Council on Clean Transportation, a latest supersonic airliner would “burn five to seven times as much fuel per passenger as a comparable subsonic jet.” Boom Supersonic states Overture will be able to run entirely on sustainable aviation fuel, but airlines, not manufacturers, decide what goes in the tank.

As Popular Science’s Bill Sweetman wrote in 2002, if you can afford a supersonic jet, “you’re not worried about a few lousy tons of fuel.” But everyone below will bear the cost of supersonic jetsetters’ small travel-time benefit in excess noise and climate-warming emissions.

According to recent reports, shurcliff saw this attempt to relax the rules coming. “Once they start flying, they’re going to want to fly them everywhere,” he told The Latest York Times in 1967, warning that over-water routes would be “like a foot in the door.” Fifty-nine years later, thanks to the FAA, the door is swinging open. It’s up to us to decide whether we’re prepared to live with the repercussions or push back as Shurcliff did more than half a century ago.

Voyager 1 is officially one light-day away from Earth

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1021 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After traveling through space for almost 50 years, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft should be one light-day away from Earth.
  • William Kurth, a research scientist at the University of Iowa who has worked on the Voyager mission since 1974 tells Popular Science that this mission is about more than just science.
  • Industry observers note that “The Voyager missions represent humanity’s curiosity and hunger to understand our species’ place in the universe,” he states.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After traveling through space for almost 50 years, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft should be one light-day away from Earth. The probe reached this record-breaking milestone at approximately 5:16:07 a.m. EST on Wednesday, November 18. Since takes about 24 hours to receive any signal from Voyager 1, NASA officially confirmed that it reached the distance on Thursday, November 19.

William Kurth, a research scientist at the University of Iowa who has worked on the Voyager mission since 1974 tells Popular Science that this mission is about more than just science.

Industry observers note that “The Voyager missions represent humanity’s curiosity and hunger to understand our species’ place in the universe,” he states. “They show that we are explorers and can work together to do wonderful things.”.

Astronomers often describe vast cosmic distances in light-years. It’s arguably the most famous unit of measurement when talking about the universe, in part because of its sheer incomprehensibility. A single particle of light travels at a speed of about 186,282 miles per second. Hypothetically speaking, if you fired a beam of light into the night sky at the outset of reading this story, it would travel around 44.7 million miles into space by the time you finished.

But even a unit like a light-minute isn’t particularly useful to astronomers. For them, cosmic measurements only start making sense on a scale of light-years. Voyager 1 is nowhere close to a light-year away from Earth, but a light-day (approximately 16,094,799,105 miles) is still basically impossible to envision as a distance. And since radio communications travel at nearly the speed of light, any messages to and from the spacecraft will require about 24 (Earth) hours to receive.

“Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” Dave Gallagher, the director of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, said in an emailed statement confirming the milestone. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward upcoming frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.”.

Even at one light-day from Earth, Voyager 1 isn’t done just yet. While several of its instruments are no longer functioning, it still routinely sends back invaluable information from its vantage point beyond the solar system.

“Voyager 1 is telling us about our sun’s interaction with its galactic neighborhood. It has told us about the amount of galactic cosmic rays, unfiltered by the sun’s magnetic field,” states Kurth. “We are learning about the variation of plasma density in the interstellar medium just outside the heliosphere (sun’s extended atmosphere). We’re anxious to see where the direction of the magnetic field rotates from one similar to the heliospheric direction to that of the pristine interstellar medium.”.

“Though it might be a long shot, I hope to see Voyager 1 crossing into the predicted hot hydrogen wall,” Adam Szabo, a Project Investigator on Voyager’s Magnetometer Experiment, tells Popular Science. “The wall is composed of neutral hydrogen atoms, so it will not register easily, but it must have some magnetic and plasma wave signature.”.

Voyager 1 released on September 5, 1977, heading for Jupiter and Saturn. Voyager 1 has 10 scientific instruments onboard, including two Golden Records engraved with sights, sounds, and depictions of life on Earth onboard—should the probe encounter any extraterrestrial life.

In a recent development, in March 1979, the Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring around Jupiter and two new Jovian moons: Thebe and Metis. When it reached Saturn in 1980, the spacecraft spotted five new moons and a new ring called the G-ring.

As part of a concept that NASA called the Grand Tour, the Voyager mission as a whole took advantage of a once-every-175-year alignment of the outer planets for a grand tour of the solar system. Its twin spacecraft Voyager 2 later explored Neptune and Uranus.

It has been revealed that on February 17, 1998, Voyager 1 became the furthest human-made object in space, after overtaking NASA’s Pioneer 10 probe. It crossed into interstellar space in August 2012, and became the first spacecraft to cross the heliosphere. This boundary is where the influences from outside of our solar system are stronger than those from our sun.

All good things must come to an end, of course. Voyager 1 is powered by three radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) fueled by decaying plutonium-23. The isotope possesses a 87.74-year half-life, so the batteries are right now operating at around two-thirds their original strength. NASA has slowly shut down onboard equipment in recent years to conserve energy, but there will come a time when there simply isn’t enough left in the RTGs for anything to operate. Barring any technical complications, mission engineers expect to bid Voyager 1 a final farewell sometime during the 2030s.

The spacecraft may cease its work as a cosmic laboratory, but its very existence ensures it will remain a monument to humanity’s potential as it barrels forward for eons.

“Voyager 1 and its companion Voyager 2 have taught us time and again that nature is not as simple and predictable as we thought,” Kurth explains. “Voyager has always provided surprising differences from our best guesses as to what it will see in any upcoming region.”.

Additionally, Szabo adds that it has an key lesson for anyone on Earth who has ever had a dream.

Recent findings suggest that “Do not be afraid to dream substantial. In 1977, even the Grand Tour seemed like a long shot,” he states. “We did not even conceive of making it into interstellar space. Dream big.”.

In a recent development, UPDATE November 19 10:00 a.m. EST: An earlier version of this story said light moves at 186,282 feet per second. It is 186,282 miles per second. We have updated unit of measurement and apologize for the error.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GM Energy and WeaveGrid are launching a vehicle-to-grid (V2G) pilot that will let select Southern California Edison (SCE) customers send electricity from their EV batteries back to the grid. Eligible drivers could get more than $16,000 in help with equipment and installation, and earn money when the grid needs their power.

GM claims the pilot participants will be its first EV drivers in California to export power from their cars to their homes. Through the California Energy Commission, eligible customers in SCE’s Emergency Load Reduction Program can get up to $8,000 toward a GM Energy V2H system and up to $8,099 toward eligible installation costs, including connecting the system to the grid.

Chevy, GMC, and Cadillac EV drivers can use time-of-use energy management to take advantage of lower rates and may be paid for participating in eligible demand-response events. How much they save or earn depends on their rate plan, electricity use, and participation.

GM already offers managed charging through 13 utilities, and each program varies by utility.

Sources indicate that an EV battery stores direct current (DC), and your house and the grid use alternating current (AC). GM’s current home backup system uses a wall-mounted inverter to convert the power. With AC bidirectional charging, the car’s onboard inverter does the job. Moving that work into the car could make the equipment on your garage wall simpler and cheaper to install.

Not in CA, but we use solar, time of use, and EVs to minimize our energy costs. We’re not feeding power back to the grid from our cars, but the combo of TOU, solar and EVs does allow us to reduce costs significantly. Solar covers all the expensive peak power, I have the cars start charging early enough to use any extra solar, and the rest is off peak at half cost.

GM is joining CharIN‘s North American AC V2G task force, which is working to align technical standards, equipment certification, and utility approval requirements. In Southern California, the pilot will give GM and its partners a look at how the process works for drivers, from signing up and getting the hardware installed to getting utility approval and sending power back.

How This Former Weightlifter Lost 80 Pounds After GLP-1s Stopped Working

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, for years, Dana Bichler was a competitive weightlifter.
  • “I tried running, and a few other things, and the weight just crept up,” he told Healthline.
  • In a recent development, dieting allowed him to lose about 50 pounds, but he would then regain it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for years, Dana Bichler was a competitive weightlifter. He felt fit and strong competing at 200 to 210 pounds. But wear and tear on his body and aging eventually pushed him to step away from weightlifting. Without the training, he began to gain weight slowly and steadily.

“I tried running, and a few other things, and the weight just crept up,” he told Healthline.

In a recent development, dieting allowed him to lose about 50 pounds, but he would then regain it. At his heaviest, he weighed close to 300 pounds, which inspired him to visit a weight-loss clinic, where he followed a plan centered on the clinic’s foods.

In a recent development, “It’s a life of deprivation,” Bichler noted. “You just can’t live like it.”.

About five years ago, he tried a GLP-1 medication and two others a few years later. Each helped him lose weight initially but then stopped working.

“There was really no long-term positive effects or benefits that I saw,” he remarked.

However, he still takes Mounjaro for blood sugar control because he is prediabetic.

Industry observers note that A few years ago, he was diagnosed with fatty liver disease. His condition was tied to obesity and caused scarring on his liver.

Bichler understood the seriousness of the condition as his two younger sisters and his oldest brother also had fatty liver disease. His brother and youngest sister developed cirrhosis, and his brother died after the disease affected other parts of his body.

“I had to do something,” he said. “What I was doing was not working.”.

It has been revealed that from his home in St. Cloud, Minnesota, Bichler traveled to the University of Minnesota to see a hepatologist, who referred him to a gastroenterologist who had worked with Boston Scientific on the instruments used to perform endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG).

ESG is a minimally invasive weight loss procedure performed using an FDA-authorized endoscopic suturing system, such as one offered through Boston Scientific’s Endura Weight Loss Solutions.

Recent findings suggest that during ESG, a doctor passes an endoscope through the mouth and uses sutures to fold the stomach into a narrower sleeve. No portion of the stomach is removed, and there are no incisions. The smaller stomach limits how much a person can eat at once.

According to recent reports, “Patients typically go home the same day and can return to routine daily activities within two to three days,” Brian Dunkin, MD, chief medical officer at Boston Scientific, told Healthline. “For the right person, that provides another less-invasive option to consider with their healthcare professional.”.

While ESG may be a good option for some people who don’t achieve weight loss goals with GLP-1 medications, can’t tolerate them, or don’t want to stay on medication long term, Dunkin noted he doesn’t think of it as ESG versus GLP-1 drugs.

“One of the best things GLP-1 medications have done is get more people talking to their doctors about obesity and recognizing it as a chronic disease that deserves treatment,” he said.

Each approach has different benefits, risks, and side effects.

“The goal is finding the right treatment, or combination of treatments, for the right patient at the right time,” said Dunkin.

Industry observers note that ESG is indicated for adults with obesity with a BMI between 30 and 50, but Dunkin stated BMI is only part of the conversation. ESG may be an option for people who aren’t getting the weight loss results they want, who don’t want to stay on weight loss medication long term, or for whom bariatric surgery may not be appropriate or desired, he added.

“Obesity is a chronic disease that requires long-term care,” said Dunkin. “ESG is one part of that care, which is why I believe so strongly in a multidisciplinary approach. The goal is to look at the whole person and find a care initiative they can sustain over time.”.

It has been revealed that in March 2025, Bichler decided ESG was a good fit for him and received the procedure at Boston Scientific. At the time, he was 67 years old and on Medicare, which pre-approved the procedure.

“I just felt comfortable with it not being invasive, and I really needed to deal with [my weight], so I did,” he said.

When Bichler underwent ESG he weighed somewhere in the 260s. Today, he weighs 178 pounds.

While the procedure went smoothly, he said the following month was difficult. Because bread, pasta, rice, and carbonated drinks were off the table, he had to consume clear liquids, then slowly moved to other liquids, and eventually cream soups.

“I found that extremely difficult,” he mentioned.

What surprised him most was depression. Looking back, he calls it a perfect storm. Working with his weight loss doctor, he had stopped taking his antidepressant about two weeks before the procedure. After surgery, his eating habits changed dramatically, disrupting the social life he’d built around food.

“I was in a pretty deep funk for a while,” he said. “I really was.”.

He restarted his antidepressant, and over time, he adjusted to a fresh way of eating.

“I’ve discovered I like cream soup,” he remarked. “I still have it for meals.”.

Although he’s lost more than 80 pounds, Bichler stated the bigger change is how good he feels. He exercises four to five days a week and has more energy and moves more easily than he has in years.

According to recent reports, “I haven’t felt this good in 30 years,” Bichler said. “I’m not kidding you.”.

According to recent reports, he’s able to enjoy things he loves like working on the farm he and his wife own. At the farm, he hunts ducks, turkeys, pheasants, and small game, and runs a trapline, all activities his weight had made nearly impossible for a long time.

“It used to be really hard for me to do because of the physicality of doing some of these things,” he said.

It has been revealed that although he retired from his profession, Bichler said he’s busier than ever. He’s a protodeacon in the Eastern Orthodox Church and also serves as a chaplain for his local police department, a role that has him climbing in and out of squad cars and up and down steps.

“Before I’d be sucking air trying to keep up,” he mentioned.

Most meaningful of all is that he has more energy to give to his family.

“I have a grandson that I can actually do things and be active with now,” Bichler said. “It’s like starting all over. I just feel like a new person.”.

Tech Report: Prickly pears can generate solar electricity

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (579 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most plants rely on real-time photosynthesis for food, which means they aren’t generating energy unless the sun is out.
  • Plants generally absorb carbon dioxide through pores in their leaves, but the prickly pear can’t afford such an evolutionary luxury.
  • Industry observers note that environmental biologists certainly did.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most plants rely on real-time photosynthesis for food, which means they aren’t generating energy unless the sun is out. Meanwhile, cacti like the prickly pear must get creative in order to survive the harsh conditions they live in. With high temperatures and little water, these plants and similar species like aloe and pineapple evolved a specialized process called crassulacean acid metabolism (CAM). The overall principles are the same, but instead of converting carbon dioxide (CO₂) and water into sugars solely during daylight, CAM allows a prickly pear to extend its photosynthesis over a full 24 hours.

Plants generally absorb carbon dioxide through pores in their leaves, but the prickly pear can’t afford such an evolutionary luxury. The desert heat would turn those same tiny openings into water drains. With CAM, a prickly pear only absorbs carbon dioxide at night, and subsequently turns it into malic acid. Photosynthesis later breaks down the acid—but only on the side of the plant directly exposed to sunlight. The shady side retains its malic acid, creating a pH concentration gradient. Interestingly, this pH imbalance is also one of the underlying principles for generating electricity…see where this is going?

Industry observers note that environmental biologists certainly did. In a study published today in the journal Plants, People, Planet, a team at the University of California, Santa Cruz, (UC Santa Cruz) detailed a new, interdisciplinary system that transforms the common prickly pear into a green solar panel. Although prickly pear voltages aren’t enough to deliver a noticeable jolt, they are strong enough to power the tiny sensors often used by farmers to monitor their crops. With some additional fine-tuning, their novel methods could offer a promising, sustainable adaptation to ongoing climate concerns.

“It was just so nice to have 10 students in a room from all across campus working together on a single project. When we’re looking at climate solutions, that’s what we need,” Charlie Chesney, a UC Santa Cruz environmental scientist and study co-author, said in a statement.

Sources indicate that wiring a single spiky plant doesn’t do much, but linking them together adds up. As few as eight prickly pears are enough to generate 4.5 volts of electricity—nearly three times the charge of a commercial AA battery. That’s more than enough to power the common, low-energy sensors used to assess plants.

“There are many commercial applications of cacti [for] monitoring their health using a low-power system like ours, that is just operating off on the side and is self-powered,” explained UC Santa Cruz ecologist and study co-author Michael Loik.

He offered one such scenario, where wired prickly pears function as organic “sentinels” that monitor field conditions and relay the information back to a farmer’s office.

“This could be a really interesting avenue to pursue,” he added.

Industry observers note that the idea isn’t limited to the prickly pear, either. Any plant that uses CAM—aloe, pineapple, agave—could benefit from a similar battery upgrade. The team even assessed how the cacti performed under a standard desert challenge like drought. Even after 15 months without water, sample prickly pears weren’t simply surviving—they were still photosynthesizing. In some cases, the resultant voltages were higher than watered control plants.

“This was a really surprising result, but also demonstrated how resilient a cactus is—it could still produce electricity even when it seems, to us, like it’s near death,” added Chesney.
